JTBD-1 is session *plus* weekly: an account at 4% session and 100% weekly has no room. `MenuBarManager` never reads `weeklyPercentage`; the only capacity test is `effectiveSessionPercentage < 100.0` (4225-4229). The risk section guards only the unmeasured-equals-0% trap, not a measured profile ranked wrong. The 10x claim rests on two surfaces the owner has never exercised. title: Consent-gated read of the claude.ai session key from Chrome during setup
critic_objection: The consent sheet cannot honestly describe the grant. Decrypting the claude.ai cookie requires Chrome's "Chrome Safe Storage" login-Keychain item — on macOS that one passphrase is the `os_crypt` key for *every* Chrome cookie and the saved-password store. The macOS prompt the brief cites as its safety feature offers "Always Allow", permanently adding RevvyTach to that item's ACL, surviving updates and uninstall. So "reads only `sessionKey`, once" is intent enforced solely by our own code, while the capability acquired is Chrome's whole secret store. Unlike a wrong number, a granted ACL cannot be un-granted by an update — and `docs/data-and-privacy.md:73-74` promises the opposite. Value is thin: skippable, org-only, no ranked job. VERDICT: SURVIVABLE only with Chrome-wide disclosure steering to "Allow".
author_response: Both citations hold verbatim: `SetupWizardView.swift:16-17` says the browser sign-in "is skippable" and adds only the org extra-usage row and org name; `data-and-privacy.md:73-74` reads "It never reads Chrome cookies, login databases, browser history, or account identifiers." The Chrome-wide scope holds too — `os_crypt` uses the one Safe Storage key for cookies and saved passwords. I accept risk 4→5 (0.45→0.36) and rewrote the first slice: disclose that scope in plain words and steer to "Allow", never "Always Allow". title: Adopt existing ~/.claude-accounts sign-ins as profiles in one click
critic_objection: `~/.claude-accounts/` is not a convention developers hand-roll into — it is RevvyTach's own directory, created by this app (`ClaudeSwitchService.swift:12-14, 29-31`). Anyone who rolled their own `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` setup used their own path, which this feature never sees, so the cohort is close to empty. What actually populates "a usable sign-in owned by no profile" is the app's own debris: `ProfileManager.deleteProfile` (`:926-1014`) scrubs secrets, history and usage but never calls `unlinkAccount`, so every deleted Claude profile leaves its directory and live login behind. On a seven-profile machine the list mostly says "recreate the profile you deliberately deleted" — with no identity shown, since the Keychain filter proves a token is usable, not whose. That is failure mode 2 offered as a button.
author_response: DROPPED — objection wins.
